data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms as a methodological rule to maximize informational content and risk asymmetry, without smuggling in induction.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper explicitly stated that choosing a theory implies an expectation of its future truth or probability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference for corroboration cannot be distinguished from a probabilistic assessment of future performance.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the framework requires a guarantee of success to justify any action, rendering 'educated guesswork' indefensible.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical status of a theory (which remains unproven) and the pragmatic decision of which theory to test or act upon. Choosing the better-corroborated theory is not a prediction of future success (induction) but a commitment to the theory with the highest empirical content and severity of testing so far. This functions as a 'regulative ideal' where the agent accepts the risk of falsification in exchange for higher potential information gain, acknowledging that acting on less corroborated theories offers no such strategic advantage.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
